title: Solar Constant and Surface Temperature of the Sun
short_intro: The solar constant is the amount of radiant energy received per unit time on a unit area surface perpendicular to the Sun's rays at the mean Earth-Sun distance. It represents the extraterrestrial solar irradiance outside the Earth's atmosphere.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Definition, numerical value, units, basic Stefan-Boltzmann law application to find solar temperature, and inverse square law dependence.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Derivation of solar constant from Stefan-Boltzmann law, angular diameter of the Sun, atmospheric absorption corrections, and spectral distribution considerations.

prerequisites: Inverse square law of radiation intensity
Concept of Temperature and blackbody approximation

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Standard Value
bullets: The solar constant (denoted by S) is defined as the total radiant energy received per second per unit normal area at the outer boundary of the Earth's atmosphere.
The globally accepted mean value of the solar constant is approximately 1.367 kW/m² or 1367 W/m².
It fluctuates by about ±3.3% due to the eccentricity of Earth's elliptical orbit around the Sun (perihelion and aphelion).

concept_notes.heading: Inverse Square Law Dependence
bullets: Total energy emitted per second by the Sun is distributed uniformly over a sphere of radius equal to the mean Earth-Sun distance (R).
The intensity of radiation decreases inversely as the square of the distance from the source.
S = (L) / (4 π R²), where L is the total luminosity of the Sun.

concept_notes.heading: Determination of Solar Temperature
bullets: Treating the Sun as a blackbody of radius r at absolute temperature T, its total emissive power is given by Stefan-Boltzmann law.
By equating the total energy emitted by the Sun's surface to the energy intercepted at radius R, the effective surface temperature T can be calculated.
The calculated effective temperature of the photosphere is approximately 5778 K (~5800 K).

concept_notes.heading: Atmospheric Effects and Terrestrial Insolation
bullets: Part of the incoming solar radiation is absorbed, scattered, and reflected by atmospheric gases, water vapor, and dust particles.
Only about 51% of the total solar radiation reaches the Earth's surface directly or diffusely.
Instruments used to measure the solar constant on Earth's surface include pyrheliometers and pyranometers, combined with atmospheric correction factors.

derivations.title: Relation between Solar Constant and Solar Temperature
derivations.conditions: Assuming the Sun behaves as a perfect blackbody of radius r at temperature T, and Earth is at a mean distance R from the Sun.
steps: Step 1: Write the total energy emitted per second by the Sun using Stefan-Boltzmann law: E = 4 pi r^2 sigma T^4

Step 2: Assume this energy spreads uniformly over a spherical shell of radius R centered at the Sun. The intensity at distance R is the solar constant S: S = \frac{4 pi r^2 sigma T^4}{4 pi R^2} = sigma T^4 left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2
Step 3: Rearrange the expression to solve for the surface temperature of the Sun: T^4 = \frac{S R^2}{sigma r^2}
Step 4: Take the fourth root on both sides to obtain the final formula for T: T = left(\frac{S R^2}{sigma r^2}\right)^{1/4}

derivations.title: Expression in terms of Angular Radius of the Sun
derivations.conditions: Using the angular subtended radius θ of the Sun from Earth.
steps: Step 1: The ratio of the Sun's radius r to the Earth-Sun distance R is equal to the sine of the angular radius (θ) of the Sun: sin\theta approx \frac{r}{R}
Step 2: Substitute this geometric relation into the solar constant equation S = sigma T^4 (\frac{r}{R})^2: S = sigma T^4 (sin\theta)^2
Step 3: For very small angles, substitute sin\theta approx \theta in radians: S = sigma T^4 \theta^2
Step 4: Express temperature in terms of S and θ: T = left(\frac{S}{sigma \theta^2}\right)^{1/4}

graphs_and_experiments.title: Spectral Energy Distribution of Solar Radiation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A bell-like asymmetric intensity vs. wavelength (λ) curve peaking in the visible region (~500 nm), comparing extraterrestrial spectrum (blackbody curve at ~5800 K) with the spectrum at sea level showing absorption bands due to H_2O, CO_2, and O_3.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that the Sun radiates like a blackbody at 5800 K, but atmospheric gases selectively absorb specific infrared and ultraviolet wavelengths.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in PGT to explain atmospheric absorption bands and blackbody radiation laws.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Angstrom Pyrheliometer Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Schematic setup of two identical manganin strips, one exposed to direct sunlight and the other heated electrically until thermal equilibrium is established using a thermocouple galvanometer null indicator.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Equates the electrical heating power per unit area to the solar radiation power absorbed by the strip, allowing precise measurement of the solar constant.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in descriptive questions for laboratory-based thermal physics experiments.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of Solar Constant with Earth's Orbit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: An annual sinusoidal or inverse-square variation curve of solar irradiance against months of the year, showing maximum value in January (perihelion) and minimum in July (aphelion).
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Proves the orbital eccentricity of Earth alters the Sun-Earth distance and hence modulates the received solar flux by about ±3.3%.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: TGT conceptual MCQs regarding seasonal solar flux variation.

solved_numericals.question: If the solar constant is 1.4 kW/m² and the mean radius of the Earth is 6400 km, calculate the total solar power intercepted by the Earth.
solution_steps: Step 1: Identify given values: S = 1.4 kW/m^2 = 1400 W/m^2, R_e = 6400 km = 6.4 \times 10^6 m.
Step 2: Use formula for intercepted power: P = S pi R_e^2.

solved_numericals.question: Assuming the Sun is a blackbody of radius 7 \times 10^8 m and the solar constant is 1367 W/m^2 at a distance of 1.5 \times 10^{11} m, find the effective surface temperature of the Sun. (Stefan-Boltzmann constant σ = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} W/m^2 K^4)
solution_steps: Step 1: Use the temperature formula: T = left(\frac{S R^2}{sigma r^2}\right)^{1/4}
Step 2: Substitute the given values: S = 1367, R = 1.5 \times 10^{11}, r = 7 \times 10^8, sigma = 5.67 \times 10^{-8}.
Step 4: Take the fourth root: T = (1.107 \times 10^{15})^{1/4} approx 5778 K.

solved_numericals.question: The angular diameter of the Sun subtended at the Earth is approximately 32 minutes of arc (0.0093 radians, or angular radius \theta = 4.65 \times 10^{-3} rad). If the solar constant is 1367 W/m² and σ = 5.67 \times 10^{-8} SI units, estimate the surface temperature of the Sun.
solution_steps: Step 1: Use angular radius formula: T = left(\frac{S}{sigma \theta^2}\right)^{1/4}
Step 5: Compute fourth root: T = (1.115 \times 10^{15})^{1/4} = 5782 K.

assumptions_and_limitations: The Sun is assumed to radiate as a uniform, ideal blackbody radiator, which neglects local variations like sunspots and solar flares.
Atmospheric transmission losses are assumed constant or corrected via standard coefficients, though local weather and humidity cause real-time variations.
The Earth's orbit is treated as circular in basic calculations, ignoring the actual orbital eccentricity when precise instantaneous values are required.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The solar constant is strictly constant and never changes throughout the year.
common_misconceptions.correct: The solar constant varies by about ±3.3% annually because Earth's orbit is elliptical.
common_misconceptions.why: Earth is closer to the Sun in January (perihelion) and farther in July (aphelion), changing the received intensity.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The solar constant is measured directly on the ground.
common_misconceptions.correct: The solar constant is defined outside the Earth's atmosphere.
common_misconceptions.why: Atmospheric absorption and scattering filter out a significant portion of solar radiation before it reaches sea level.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The entire surface of the Earth receives the solar constant flux simultaneously.
common_misconceptions.correct: Only a cross-sectional disc area (π R_e^2) receives direct beam flux, and when averaged over the entire spherical surface, the flux is S/4.
common_misconceptions.why: Spherical geometry distributes the incoming solar energy over a surface area four times larger than its cross-sectional projection.

quick_revision: Solar constant S equals approximately 1367 W/m² outside the Earth's atmosphere.
The inverse square law governs how solar radiation intensity drops with distance from the Sun: S proportional to 1 / R².
Sun's effective surface temperature is calculated using Stefan-Boltzmann law as T = (S / (σ θ²))^{1/4} ≈ 5800 K.
Average solar radiation received over the entire Earth surface is S/4 due to spherical geometry.
